finalMixedAudioReview.transcript: 1. Your tests pass. Then a worker dies and a job never comes back. RaceLab reproduces the failure and checks a meta-generated repair built by Tang Vu during this hackathon using earlier Ten source and event infrastructure. This is a real TypeScript method from a pinned public repository. It runs against a real disposable database inside a separate worker process. Claim the job, commit the row, stop the worker. The database survives. The original method leaves the job claimed. Now start a replacement worker on the same database. The trace shows exactly what committed, and when the old process exited. The original misses the claimed row. The repair reclaims it after the declared sixty-second lease, without changing its payload. Meta's model sees the source and the contract, then chooses a crash probe. The tool returns an actual failure. Next, Meta writes a candidate method. Independent code executes and scores it. Open the hypothesis, feedback, and diff. The model never awards itself a pass. But recovering one job is only half the story. A worker may still be alive. Or it may return with an old token. The life cycle adapter tests contention, interruption, renewal, and stale ownership. Both feedback candidates pass all ten conditions, with guards inside their source. A good experiment needs controls, not just a green badge. Unchanged OpenMusic code passes in fourteen bounded checks. The error rules diff function meets six of eight checks. It fails two under our added line edit contract. These are source adapters, not full application runs or human feedback. We also compare direct repair with repair using executed feedback. Across twelve attempts, feedback passes six of six, direct four of six. Failures include truncation and an invented SQL column. Seven previously unrun attempts were collected later under a separately frozen continuation. This small study proves no general superiority. Inspect the evidence online.
